children.text: Completed in

, it is the oldest stone church in the Philippines, having survived earthquakes and war to earn a place on the UNESCO World Heritage List. A trompe-l'oeil ceiling, a museum in the former monastery and the tomb of Manila's founder, Legazpi, are all gathered in one place.
San Agustin Church is an Augustinian church standing on General Luna Street in Intramuros, Manila's walled city. The first church on this spot, built in
, was a modest chapel of bamboo and nipa palm, and it burned down in
December 1574
. A second church, rebuilt in wood, was lost in
February 1583
. So in
the friars began building in stone to a design by Juan Macías, and finished the work on
January 19, 1607
The Latin-cross building, about
long and

wide, is built of stone quarried at Meycauayan in Bulacan and at Binangonan and San Mateo in Rizal. Its walls are thick and buttressed on the sides, and a stone barrel vault and a dome roof it, all designed to withstand earthquakes; its style is said to follow the Augustinian churches of Mexico. It remains a living church today, an Immaculate Conception parish and the archdiocesan shrine of Our Lady of Consolation and the Cincture, where Mass is still celebrated.
The church's history reads like a record of disasters. It lived through major earthquakes from 1645 to 1880, and in the quake of
June 3, 1863
it is said to have been the only public building in Manila left undamaged. The
quake cracked a bell tower badly and one tower was taken down, which is why only one stands on the façade today. In the Battle of Manila in
it was the only one of Intramuros's seven churches to survive (the neighboring monastery was completely destroyed), and in
it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as one of the "Baroque Churches of the Philippines," together with
Paoay Church
Santa Maria Church
and
Miagao Church

The outside is sturdy, plain gray stone, but once you step through the door, a ceiling and walls painted in trompe-l'oeil astonish many visitors. It suits travelers interested in architecture, religious art and Philippine colonial history, people looking for a cool interior to escape the midday heat, and anyone who enjoys photography. The story of the whole walled city is told in the
Intramuros
entry; this entry focuses on a close look inside the church and museum.
The ceiling and walls were painted by the Italian artists Cesare Alberoni and Giovanni Dibella, who were commissioned in

. The moldings, rosettes and recessed coffered panels are all brushwork on a flat surface, yet they look as if they stand out like carved plaster. The sense of depth changes as you look up from the middle of the nave, from near the entrance and from close to the altar.

The 18th-century main door, made of molave wood, is crowded with carved saints, including St. Augustine and St. Monica, and with rococo-style vines and flowers. Before you go in, pause at the door and take your time looking up to the heights you cannot reach.
On the upper floor above the entrance are 68 wooden choir stalls covered in dense carved patterns, and beside them stands an old pipe organ. The stalls were restored between
by the Escuela Taller de Filipinas Foundation. This area is part of the museum route, and whether it is open can vary from day to day.

Above the aisle that runs through the nave hang several large crystal chandeliers said to have been brought from Paris, and at the far end a golden altar screen (retablo) glows. Together with the checkerboard floor, this is the spot where photos come out best.
This is the old monastery building next to the church. It was converted into a museum in the
to a design by the architect Angel Nakpil and opened in

. In the cloisters, friars' rooms, sacristy and refectory you will see religious paintings, vestments, statues, furniture, large choir books and ceramics from the Spanish colonial period. In one spot you can see the church's bell tower through a capiz (shell) window.

At the heart of the museum is a square courtyard with palm trees, a fountain and low hedged flower beds. On a rainy day it is a pleasant place to rest under the cloister eaves and listen to the rain. The complex also has a garden named after Francisco Manuel Blanco, an Augustinian friar and botanist.

People buried in this church include Miguel López de Legazpi, who founded Manila, the conquistador Juan de Salcedo, the painter Juan Luna, the food scientist María Orosa and the historian Teodoro Agoncillo. The burial places lie in the crypt and in a side chapel, and how much is open to the public varies over time, so ask at the entrance.

blocks.title: Our Lady of Consolation and the Cincture

children.text: This is the church's patron image of Mary, which received a formal canonical coronation with the Holy See's approval on
September 4, 2000
. Around the Marian feast each September, an event is held in which the statue is placed on a carriage (carroza), and on
September 8, 2024
the first "Fiesta de Intramuros" honoring this devotion was held.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Focus on the church and museum

children.text: Arrive at the plaza in front of the church and first look at the façade, bell tower and the carvings on the main door from the outside. A weekday morning with no Mass is quiet.
Go inside and take in the whole ceiling, the chandeliers and the altar. If a wedding or funeral is under way, watch quietly from the back.
Buy a ticket at the museum ticket counter and, if possible, go around with a guide: cloisters, sacristy, refectory, then the choir loft. It usually takes
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
Walk once around the courtyard garden and stop by the museum gift shop.
The museum closes for lunch, so come out and eat at a restaurant on General Luna Street.
With the time left, walk on across the street to sights of
Intramuros
such as Casa Manila and Manila Cathedral.

Watch the sunset from the wall walk, and on the way back see the church façade once more after dark.
On days when the church interior is closed or restricted, tour the museum first, check when the ceremony ends, and then see the nave. On Sundays, avoid the
Mass and go in after
. On rainy days, spend more time in the museum cloisters and take your photos of the façade early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

items.title: From central Manila by jeepney or LRT

children.text: From LRT-1 Carriedo or Doroteo Jose station, a jeepney toward Manila Cathedral takes about
10–15 minutes
and costs about
. Get off in front of Manila Cathedral and walk along General Luna Street for about
5–10 minutes
to reach the church façade.
You can also get off at LRT-1 Central Terminal station and walk to the wall entrance. The fare is about
depending on the distance, and it is very crowded at rush hour.
It is about
10 km
from Ninoy Aquino International Airport, taking
30 minutes–1 hour 20 minutes
depending on traffic, and a Grab costs about
From Makati or BGC it takes about
30 minutes–1 hour
and costs about
. Enter "San Agustin Church, General Luna Street" as your destination and you will be taken to the plaza in front of the church.

There is parking near the plaza in front of the church, but spaces are limited and it gets crowded during Masses, ceremonies and events, so check the fee and availability on site. Traffic in Manila is heavy, so Grab or public transport is more convenient if possible.
It is about
5–10 minutes
on foot from Manila Cathedral and about
10–15 minutes
from Fort Santiago. The cobbled streets inside the walls are flat, but there is little shade at midday, so bring a hat and water.
Inside the church you are sheltered from rain and sun, so it is good to visit all year, but the walk to the church and the courtyard depend on the weather.
December–February
is relatively cool and dry, which makes it most comfortable to walk the plaza in front of the church and the cloister.
March–May
brings midday temperatures up to around
, so move in the early morning or late afternoon and spend midday inside the church and museum.
June–November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and
July–September

is affected by typhoons. In heavy rain the road in front of the church can flood and some plans are cancelled, so check the forecast. Seasonal events include the Christmas season with the dawn and evening Masses called "Simbang Gabi," held
December 16–24
; Holy Week (usually
late March–April

), with a Good Friday procession that starts from the church; and the Marian feast around September. These periods make the church beautiful, but it gets crowded and general visiting may be restricted.

There are few places to stay inside the walls around the church, so most travelers stay in Ermita/Malate (about
10–15 minutes
by car, about
a night) or in Makati/BGC and visit as a day trip. A hotel inside the walls is convenient if you want to see both the early-morning light and the church at night, but the price is high, at about
a night, so check before booking.

After the church, a long-established restaurant along General Luna Street is a good place for lunch with Filipino home cooking such as sinigang, adobo and lechon kawali. Barbara's, a long-running restaurant in Intramuros, is known for a buffet with traditional performances. On a hot afternoon, try halo-halo or calamansi juice, and for gifts, the museum shop's devotional items and postcards or Intramuros handicrafts are good choices.
The museum is open
and
and closes from noon to 1 p.m. It is safest to go in before lunchtime and allow
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
. Open days and hours may change, so check the latest announcement.
On weekdays, Mass is listed at
and
, and on Sundays an English Mass at

is given consistently across sources. The other times on Saturdays and Sundays, and the times during Holy Week and on feast days, differ between sources or change, so check the latest schedule and refrain from sightseeing during Mass.
This is a church where many weddings are held. On a wedding day, access to the nave is restricted, so it is a good idea to call the church office (tel. +63 2 8527 2746) before you go.
The church is a place of worship. Avoid sleeveless tops and short pants, and silence your phone. Do not take photos where a no-photography sign is posted.
Ask at the museum entrance how to use a guide and what it costs; a guide will help you understand the monastery's history and the exhibits much better. Explanations are mainly in English.

For the ceiling, rather than shooting straight up from the front, step back a little from the middle of the aisle and use a wide-angle lens to capture the depth. Avoid tripods, as they get in the way of others.
Carrying coins and small notes (₱20–100) is handy for jeepneys, lighting candles and buying devotional items.
Seeing the church and the museum together usually takes
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
. If you plan to combine it with Fort Santiago or Manila Cathedral, see the church first in the morning.
This is a working church where Mass and ceremonies take place. Access may be restricted or suspended during a ceremony, so leave some slack in your schedule in case you have to wait an hour or more.
The ceiling paintings, walls, wooden doors and choir stalls are very old, so do not touch them or lean on them. Do not use a flash when taking photos.
The plaza in front of the church and the roads inside the walls may have touts and pickpockets. Carry your bag in front and do not walk with your phone in your hand.
The midday sun is strong and there is a risk of heatstroke. Look for shade when you queue outside the church, and drink plenty of water.
Inside the church there are dark areas and uneven floors, so the elderly and children should watch their step. The stone floor is slippery in the rain.
Museum collections, the layout of exhibits and whether some areas are open can change at any time. If this guide differs from the signs on site, follow the signs on site.
About
5–10 minutes
on foot. This cathedral stands on Plaza Roma at the center of Intramuros; its stained glass and pipe organ are impressive, and admission is free.
About
15 minutes
on foot. A museum complex with art, anthropology and natural history exhibits, it makes an interesting comparison with the religious art you saw in the church.
About
15–20 minutes
on foot. A symbolic park of Manila with the Jose Rizal monument and a broad lawn.
About
10–15 minutes
by Grab. Having lunch or dinner in what is known as the world's oldest Chinatown makes a great pairing.
About
20–30 minutes
by Grab. A Gothic-style church with a steel structure; though also Catholic architecture, it has a completely different atmosphere from San Agustin Church.
